slides.title: Parcelbird Now: should we launch quick-commerce grocery delivery in 2027?
Key questions

claims.claim: Should Parcelbird launch Parcelbird Now, its own 15-minute grocery delivery service in three Midwest cities, in 2027, and still reach profit within its $12.0M of cash?
evidence: 1 Is quick commerce a market that operators can serve at a profit?
2 Can a Parcelbird dark store earn a contribution profit per order by month 18?
3 Does Parcelbird run sites and win customers better than benchmark operators?
4 Does the launch fit within today's $12.0M and 12 months of runway?
5 What should Parcelbird do in 2027 instead, and when would it look again?
Decision maker: The board (two founders, two investors), deciding to approve or reject the launch

Success criteria: A path to profitability within today's $12.0M of cash, with no new round; At least 12 months of runway at all times; A contribution profit per order by month 18, as the founders' plan promises
Timing: Board meeting, January 2027
Out of scope: Cities beyond Columbus, Indianapolis and Kansas City; Raising a new funding round; The detailed software product roadmap

slides.title: The market grows but does not pay
The market is growing fast, but no operator in it has yet shown a way to make money

evidence: 2.8x growth in US quick-commerce sales from 2022 to 2025

slides.title: 1a: Demand is real: US quick-commerce grocery sales grew 2.8 times from 2022 to 2025

claims.claim: The founders' growth claim holds
evidence: US quick-commerce grocery sales (GMV), $ billions: 2022 1.8; 2023 2.6; 2024 3.6; 2025 5.1
2.8x growth in sales over three years

claims.claim: Every year: sales grew between 38% and 44%, an average of 42% a year
No slowdown yet: 2025 grew faster than 2024, on a base twice the size of 2022
Growth is not profit: the operators selling this growth lose money on each order (1b)

slides.title: 1b: Neither incumbent makes money on an order it delivers, even at national scale

claims.claim: Zipcart: Losing money at $1.2B of revenue; Scale has not fixed the per-order loss
evidence: −$1.9 Zipcart contribution per order, national, 2025
EBITDA loss of $310M on $1,200M of revenue
A 26% EBITDA loss on each revenue dollar

claims.claim: QuickBasket: The model closest to Parcelbird Now; Regional scale loses more per order than national
evidence: −$3.4 QuickBasket contribution per order, regional, 2025
EBITDA loss of $96M on $210M of revenue
A 46% EBITDA loss on each revenue dollar

claims.claim: Retreating, not expanding; The closest precedent for a regional launch
evidence: 36.4% of QuickBasket's cities closed in 2025
4 of its 11 cities shut in a single year
Capex in closed cities is sunk

claims.claim: Growth in this market has gone to operators who lose money on it; a new regional entrant starts from a weaker position than both

slides.title: 1b: Zipcart's one profitable city shows the price of profit: a new $3.99 fee and 14% fewer orders

claims.claim: The founders cite it as proof the model works
evidence: Zipcart loses $1.90 an order across its national network
Its densest city is its best chance to make money on an order
The founders' investor update quotes only the result

claims.claim: Profit came from charging customers more
evidence: Added a $3.99 service fee to every order
Cut promotions to 1% of order value
Accepted the fall in orders that followed

claims.claim: Impact
evidence: $0.4 contribution per order after the changes
$3.99 new service fee, twice Parcelbird's planned $1.99 fee
−14% change in order volume in that city

slides.title: 2a: Even the best basket and best density, never seen at one site, would still lose $1.8 an order

slides.title: 2b: Nearly half of the plan's gain per order, 46%, depends on inputs beyond the best site ever observed

evidence: Gain per order, $: Orders per rider-hour 2.4 to 3.5: 2.3244; AOV $34 to $45: 2.31; Promotions 6% to 2% of AOV: 1.8; Orders per site per day 900 to 1,800: 1.7504
46.1% of the gain needs inputs no site has reached

claims.claim: Rider productivity and AOV: the two largest steps, and both sit above the best site
Promotions: a third of the benchmark rate, while the pop-up ran at 12% (3a)

slides.title: 2b: Each of the plan's four key inputs is set above the best benchmark site, rider productivity most of all

claims.claim: Each of the plan's four key inputs is set above the best benchmark site, rider productivity most of all
evidence: Average order value: median $34, best $42, plan $45 — 7% above the best, 32% above the median
Promotions, % of AOV: 6%, 6%, 2% — A third of every site's rate; the pop-up paid 12%
Orders per rider-hour: 2.4, 3, 3.5 — Furthest from evidence / 17% above the best site, whose 3.0 is also the top of the 1.9–3.0 range
Orders per site per day: 900, 1,400, 1,800 — 29% above the top of the 400–1,400 range
Best AOV and best density come from different sites; no site achieved both

slides.title: 2c: Copying Zipcart's fix would still leave a median site losing $1.05 an order once volume falls

claims.claim: The test is generous to the fix, and it still fails
evidence: −$2.7 order margin at the median before site costs (2a)
+ $3.99 Zipcart's new service fee on every order
+ $1.7 promotions cut from 6% to 1% of a $34 order
− $4.1 site fixed cost per order once volume falls 14% to 774 a day
= −$1.05 contribution per order with Zipcart's pricing
Rider productivity is held at 2.4 orders an hour although fewer orders means longer trips
Customers who stay keep a $34 basket after paying the new fee
With no volume loss at all, the site would still lose $0.48 an order
A site would need 1,042 orders a day at these prices to break even, above the 900 median

slides.title: 2d: With two launch cities weighing pay floors, the plan absorbs rider cost only up to $24.8 an hour

claims.claim: A 40% rise in rider cost would erase the plan's profit
evidence: $5.1 rider cost per order in the plan: $17.75 an hour ÷ 3.5 orders
+ $2.02 plan contribution per order
= $7.1 highest rider cost per order before the plan loses money
× 3.5 orders per rider-hour in the plan
= $24.8 rider cost an hour at which the plan breaks even

claims.claim: Two of the three launch cities are considering minimum pay standards for delivery workers
evidence: The briefing pack does not say how high those standards would be

claims.claim: At the median's 2.4 orders an hour, a site breaks even only if riders cost $2.95 an hour
evidence: Every other input is held at the plan's values, all above the best site (2b)

slides.title: The market grows but does not pay

slides.title: 3a: Even after six weeks of fast growth, the pop-up ended at about 400 orders a day, under half the median

slides.title: 3b: Stated demand did not hold: 44% of young adults said weekly, yet 22% of customers still ordered by month three

Pay standard levels: How high the proposed rider minimum pay would be — The plan already breaks even only below $24.8 an hour (2d)
What the $9.5M covers: Whether it includes the software business's burn — Both readings break the runway rule (4a)
Pop-up cost detail: Its own picking, payment and margin figures — Density and promotions alone put it below the median (3a)
Monthly ramp of the plan: Store openings and volume month by month — Even full-year plan inputs need above-best performance (2b)

slides.title: Next steps

normalized.recommendation: Do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027; grow the software business instead (hire 2 engineers and 2 sales, close the 9 late-stage grocer deals, support grocers' fast delivery from stores); revisit only if a real site passes four gates, reviewed at the Q4 2027 board review.

alternatives_considered.option: Trial one own dark store first
alternatives_considered.treatment: Not now: a median store loses about $2.0M a year (4b); a trial store would also put Parcelbird in competition with the grocers it sells to (5b)
Recommended: late-stage deals cover the hires (5a); only path that meets both of the board's conditions

alternatives_considered.option: Copy Zipcart's fix ($3.99 service fee, promotions cut to 1%)
alternatives_considered.treatment: Would still leave a median site losing $1.05 an order once volume falls 14%; break-even needs 1,042 orders a day against the 900 median
Out of scope; the lead investor calls a round for a delivery operator unlikely; today's cash treated as the limit
Out of scope: the plan covers Columbus, Indianapolis and Kansas City

assumptions_and_uncertainties: Dark stores open 365 days a year — spreads site costs as thinly as possible
Customers still ordering in month three never leave — overstates the value of each customer
Acquisition cost stays at the pop-up's $38 per customer at scale — paid channels usually cost more as they scale
Pop-up margin, fee, picking and payment take benchmark values — the test reported none of its own
Zipcart's fix: rider productivity and basket hold after the fee — understates the loss after volume falls
The $9.5M need read as covering all spending to month 18 — the kinder of the two readings
The briefing pack has no data on Midwest competitors, so the founders' claim that nobody owns the Midwest is not tested
The briefing pack does not say how high the proposed rider minimum pay standards would be
The briefing pack does not say whether the $9.5M includes the software business's own $0.4M monthly burn; both readings are shown
Pop-up cost detail (own picking, payment and margin) missing
Monthly ramp of the plan (store openings and volume month by month) missing
Six weeks is a short test; read as the starting point a new site would face, not as a steady state
Pop-up orders assumed to grow a steady 18% a week; the pack gives only the average
Runway floor uses today's burn of $0.4M a month; it would rise once stores open
Pipeline ARR assumes the average contract value of $96K a year holds for every grocer
The briefing pack does not say how many pipeline grocers plan store-based delivery, only that several do
Survey and pop-up measure different groups
Nine-store annual figures are full-year run rate with no ramp-up; exclude capex, marketing and head-office costs
Risks of the recommendation: a rival opens dark stores; pipeline slips; rider pay floors; founder focus

normalized.extraction_notes: Slide 31's option table has rating circles (Weak to Strong) for four criteria, and the extracted text doesn't include them. Only the verdict column could be captured. Slides 12 and 39 mention shading and highlighting, which also didn't come through in the text. Slides 4, 9, 17, 25 and 30 are contents dividers that all carry the title "The market grows but does not pay". Slide 37 is the appendix contents page and also repeats a backup title. Chart values were copied exactly as extracted, including unrounded ones such as 7.3958. The deck itself says on slide 1 that all its data is synthetic and fictional. There were no image files to view.
